content: Lyn, also known as LYN tyrosine-protein kinase, is a protein encoded by the LYN gene in humans. It belongs to the Src family of protein tyrosine kinases and is predominantly expressed in hematopoietic cells, neural tissues, liver, and adipose tissue. Within various hematopoietic cells, Lyn functions as a critical enzyme that regulates cell activation. A small fraction of Lyn is associated with cell surface receptor proteins, such as the B cell antigen receptor (BCR), CD40, and CD19. The name Lyn is derived from Lck/Yes novel tyrosine kinase, with Lck and Yes also being members of the Src kinase family. Function Lyn has been identified as having an inhibitory role in the proliferation of myeloid lineage cells. Upon engagement of B cell receptors, Lyn undergoes rapid phosphorylation and activation. This activation initiates a cascade of signaling events, including the phosphorylation of tyrosine residues within immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) of receptor proteins. This process subsequently recruits and activates other kinases, such as Syk, phospholipase Cγ2 (PLCγ2), and phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase. These kinases generate activation signals that are essential for processes like cell proliferation, calcium mobilization, and differentiation. Lyn also plays a pivotal role in transmitting inhibitory signals by phosphorylating tyrosine residues within immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) in regulatory proteins like CD22, PIR-B, and FcγRIIB1. ITIM phosphorylation leads to the recruitment and activation of phosphatases such as SHIP-1 and SHP-1, which downregulate signaling pathways, attenuate cell activation, and promote immune tolerance. In B cells, Lyn establishes the threshold for cell signaling and maintains a balance between activation and inhibition. Rather than acting as a binary on-off switch, Lyn functions as a rheostat, fine-tuning signaling intensity. Lyn has also been implicated in the insulin signaling pathway. Activated Lyn phosphorylates insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1), which enhances the translocation of GLUT-4 to the cell membrane and increases glucose utilization. Additionally, insulin receptor activation has been shown to increase Lyn autophosphorylation, suggesting a potential feedback loop. The insulin secretagogue glimepiride (Amaryl®) activates Lyn in adipocytes by disrupting lipid rafts, which may contribute to its extrapancreatic glycemic control effects. Tolimidone (MLR-1023), a small molecule Lyn activator, is currently under Phase 2a investigation for Type II diabetes. In June 2016, Melior Discovery, the sponsor of these studies, announced positive results from their Phase 2a trial with tolimidone in diabetic patients and plans for further clinical studies. Lyn has also been shown to protect against hepatocellular apoptosis and promote liver regeneration by preserving mitochondrial integrity in hepatocytes. Pathology Much of the current understanding of Lyn comes from studies on genetically modified mice. Lyn-deficient mice exhibit a phenotype characterized by splenomegaly, a significant increase in myeloid progenitors, and the development of monocyte/macrophage tumors. Biochemical analyses of cells from these mutants have revealed that Lyn is essential for establishing ITIM-dependent inhibitory signaling and activating specific protein tyrosine phosphatases in myeloid cells. Mice expressing a hyperactive Lyn allele are tumor-free and show no predisposition to hematological malignancies. However, these mice have reduced numbers of conventional B lymphocytes, downregulated surface immunoglobulin M (IgM) and costimulatory molecules, and increased numbers of B1a B cells. With age, these animals develop glomerulonephritis, a condition associated with a 30% reduction in life expectancy. Interactions Lyn has been shown to interact with several proteins, including c-Kit, BCAR1, CD117, CD22, Cdk1, DOK1, EPOR, GPVI, INPP5D, IRS1, LCP2, MUC1, NEDD9, PLCG2, PPP1R15A, PTPRC, Syk, TRPV4, and UNC119.
